unit.can_do_en: pick up a parcel and spell my name.

brief.situation_en: A courier, Mikael, knocks on Maria's door.

lines.speaker: Mikael
lines.text_puhe: Moi! Onks tää Leena Virtasen asunto?
lines.text_kirja: Hei! Onko tämä Leena Virtasen asunto?
lines.gloss_en: Hi! Is this Leena Virtanen's flat?

judge.reason: Moi/hei and onks/onko are register differences; same question about Leena Virtanen's apartment.

puhe.text: Moi! Onks tää Leena Virtasen asunto?

kirja.text: Hei! Onko tämä Leena Virtasen asunto?

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: No, she lives in the flat next door.

judge.reason: Spoken 'se' refers to a person, equal to written 'hän'; same meaning.

lines.speaker: Mikael
lines.text_puhe: Se ei oo kotona. Voitsä ottaa paketin?
lines.text_kirja: Hän ei ole kotona. Voitko sinä ottaa paketin?
lines.gloss_en: She's not home. Could you take the parcel?

judge.reason: Spoken 'se' is the colloquial form of 'hän' for a person, 'oo' is 'ole', and 'voit sä' is 'voitko sinä'. Negation, place and the request are the same.

puhe.text: Se ei oo kotona. Voitsä ottaa paketin?

kirja.text: Hän ei ole kotona. Voitko sinä ottaa paketin?

judge.reason: Joo and kyllä both mean yes; same reply.
Kiitti/kiitos and sun nimi/sinun nimesi are register variants; same request to write your name.
Okei/selvä and onks/onko are register differences; same question about whether it is heavy.

lines.speaker: Mikael
lines.gloss_en: A little. There are books in it.

judge.reason: Siin/siinä is a dropped ending; same statement that there are books in it.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Ei hätää. Mä annan sen Leenalle illal.
lines.text_kirja: Ei hätää. Minä annan sen Leenalle illalla.
lines.gloss_en: No worries. I'll give it to Leena this evening.

judge.reason: Mä/minä and illal/illalla are register differences; same promise to give it to Leena in the evening.

puhe.text: Ei hätää. Mä annan sen Leenalle illal.

kirja.text: Ei hätää. Minä annan sen Leenalle illalla.

forms.why_en: Moi is the everyday spoken hello. Books and formal texts write hei.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: On with -ko to ask a question. Speech often says -ks: onks.
Speech shortens tämä to tää. Books write tämä.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Ei on its own answers 'no'. People say it the same way.
Speech uses se for a person. Books write hän.
Asua 'to live' doubles its last vowel for 'she': hän asuu. People say it the same way.
Adds -ssä to match asunnossa: viereinen becomes viereisessä, the n turning to s.
Adds -ssa for 'in': asunto becomes asunnossa, nt turning to nn.
After ei the verb drops its ending: olla becomes ole. Speech shortens ole to oo.
Koti with -na means 'at home': kotona. The i of koti turns into o before the ending. You hear it every day.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 2nd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Voit with -ko asks 'can you?': voitko. Speech drops -ko and adds sä: voitsä.
Speech shortens sinä to sä. Books write sinä.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
As the whole thing you take, paketti takes -n: paketin, tt turning to t.
Joo is the everyday spoken yes. Books write kyllä.
From tosi, true. Totta kai means of course.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Kiitti is the everyday spoken thanks. Books write kiitos.
The imperative for one person drops the ending: kirjoittaa becomes kirjoita. Speech says kirjota.
Sinä with -n for 'your': sinun. Speech shortens it to sun.

forms.form_name_en: nominative singular, with the possessive ending for your
forms.why_en: Adds -si for 'your'; nimi turns its i to e first: nimesi. Speech just says sun nimi.
The illative singular of tämä 'this': tähän, 'into this place, here'.
Okei is the everyday spoken OK. Books write selvä, which means clear.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Painava means 'heavy', from painaa 'to weigh'. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
The inessive singular of se 'it': siinä. Speech drops the last ä: siin.
The form of olla, to be, for he, she or it. People say it the same way.
The partitive plural is used for some books: kirja becomes kirjoja.
The partitive after ei: ei hätää, no worries.
Speech shortens minä to mä. Books write minä.
Adds -n for 'I': antaa becomes annan, nt turning to nn.
Se with -n when the whole thing is the object: kirjoittaa sen.
Adds -lla for a time of day: ilta becomes illalla, the t turning to l. Speech shortens -lla to -l: illalla becomes illal.
